content: Different scenarios can be analyzed based on the context of various countries using the provided code. When the code displayed in Box 1 is entered into the R console, it generates a function named `nsize`. This function is minimalistic and does not include checks for invalid parameter values. It can be applied to explore different values for the acceptable threshold level of matched audited records to source documents (p), the decision threshold (d), the total number of basic management units (BMUs) in the country (N), and the Type I error rate (α = 0.05). In the Netherlands, the number of tuberculosis (TB) cases is compared against external and internal registration systems, and trends in TB cases over time are examined. Aggregated TB mortality data from the surveillance system is compared annually with death rates reported by the Central Bureau of Statistics (CBS). Increases and decreases in both systems are routinely monitored, and trends are explored when necessary. All culture-positive TB cases (approximately 70%) examined by the National Reference Laboratory are linked weekly to patients reported in the surveillance system. Treatment outcome results are integrated into the case-based surveillance system. The national data management unit validates all newly notified cases daily (real-time surveillance) and alerts authorities in case of a significant increase in new TB cases. In the event of a significant decrease, primary data sources are checked to ensure there is no under-reporting. Quarterly and annual reports are compared with previous reporting periods to identify changes in trends within TB surveillance data. This is done visually without statistical tests. In the United Kingdom, several strategies are employed to ensure internal consistency in the number of reported TB cases. Public Health England, which manages the TB surveillance system (ETS), obtains mortality data from the Office of National Statistics (ONS) weekly. These data are used to validate TB death data from the ETS annually using aggregated numbers. Trends in TB mortality over time are examined separately for ETS data (e.g., TB as the cause, contributor, incidental, or unknown relationship to death) and ONS data (e.g., TB as the underlying cause of death). In 2012, data from the two systems were linked, using all ONS records mentioning TB, not just those where TB was the underlying cause of death. Cases with an unknown relationship to death in ETS were updated using ONS data, and this procedure is now a routine consistency check. If more TB deaths are found in ONS than in ETS, regional coordinators are contacted to follow up on these cases for notification and to query treatment outcomes recorded in ETS with the clinics. In the future, laboratory isolates not regularly notified (monthly) will be matched with mortality data, as previous studies have shown a higher proportion of non-notified laboratory cases had died compared to notified cases. Patients reported in ETS are linked with culture-positive cases examined by the National Reference Laboratory. Since 2010, all drug-resistant isolates from the lab are followed up for notification with the clinics. If isolates are not matched to cases by clinics, the isolate data remain in the system indefinitely, prompting regional coordinators to follow up with clinics to notify the case. Treatment outcome results are integrated into ETS. Regional coordinators follow up on 12-month treatment outcomes annually and, as of 2013, will begin following up on all outcomes beyond 12 months. Regions within the UK compare their own regional data over time and notify the national team if sudden changes are observed. Analyses are conducted on sub-groups (e.g., chi-square tests for proportions of cases by sex, pulmonary status, UK-born status, age group, region, and history of previous treatment) comparing the current and previous year. The ratio of children to adults over time is also examined. A sudden increase or decrease in the frequency of certain variables that is unexpected would prompt an investigation into the validity of the data with reference laboratories and the software development unit. A dashboard developed with the Department of Health examines the proportion of cases completing treatment by the health protection unit and whether it meets the target of 85%. The dashboard also compares the incidence rate in the current and previous year using confidence intervals. If rates exceed the previous year or treatment outcomes fall below the target, the health protection unit (for areas with over 20 cases per year) is alerted to investigate further. In the United States, two methods are used to assess changes in TB case rates. The first method compares the reported TB cases by state within the National Tuberculosis Surveillance System (NTSS) with the verbal count each state provides to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) annually. This ensures that case counts match at both state and national levels. The second method compares the annual change in rate against the expected rate for the nation. If the national rate change is above or below the expected rate, more rigorous statistical methods and investigations may be undertaken. In 2009, an unexpected and significantly steeper decline in reported TB case counts was observed in the USA compared to recent years (an 8% decline since 2000). The CDC worked with partners to investigate whether the decline reflected changes in surveillance reporting, diagnosis, or other factors. Trends from multiple sources on TB treatment initiation, medication sales, and laboratory and genotyping data on culture-positive TB were examined. Over 142,000 incident TB cases reported to the US NTSS during January 1, 2000–December 31, 2009, were analyzed. The investigation also included analysis of TB control program data from 59 public health reporting areas, self-reported data from 50 CDC-funded public health laboratories, monthly electronic prescription claims for new TB therapy prescriptions, and complete genotyping results available for NTSS cases. Accounting for prior trends using regression and time-series analyses, the deviation between observed and expected TB cases in 2009 was calculated based on patient and clinical characteristics, and the point in time the deviation occurred was assessed. Other independent information systems (e.g., TB prescription claims and public health laboratories) reported similar patterns of declines. Genotyping data did not suggest sudden decreases in recent transmission. The assessments showed that the decline in reported TB was not an artifact of changes in surveillance methods. While the steady decline of TB cases before 2009 suggested ongoing improvement in TB control, no substantial changes in TB control activities or TB transmission that would account for the abrupt decline in 2009 were identified. Other multiple causes coinciding with the economic recession in the United States, including decreased immigration and delayed access to medical care, could be related to the TB decline.
